_comment: The judgment half of the repository map: what each part is FOR, the files
that flow through the pipeline at runtime, the cross-language hops, and the
rules that cut across modules. None of this can be parsed out of the source,
so it is written by hand here and merged on top of the derived facts by
Edit this file, then run `python tools/repo_map.py update`. Never edit
docs/repo-map.json or docs/repo-map.md directly — both are generated.
pipeline: tracker.view (the last step of every pass)

tracker/manifest.py.role: The _manifest.xlsx schema and every read/write of it. Owns RequestItem, Status, Override, load_manifest(), write_statuses() (lock-retry, then a pending-JSON sidecar merged on the next write) and create_template().
tracker/manifest.py.notes: Every other module goes through this to touch the manifest. create_template() writes ONLY the accountant's columns — scanner state is written separately by write_statuses(), which is why seeding a test fixture takes both calls. Workbook saves go through save_workbook_atomically() (write beside, os.replace) so a crash mid-save never leaves a manifest Excel cannot open; atomic_replacement() / write_text_atomically() / write_json_atomically() are the same guarantee for every sidecar, the content cache, settings.json and the schedule XML, with a temp name (temp_path_for) unique per process and write but still ending in TEMP_SUFFIX so the validators ignore it. quarantine_sidecar() never overwrites an earlier corrupt file and does nothing with quarantine=False, which is what every reader and dry run passes. identifier_problem() refuses identifiers that could not survive as a folder-name prefix (illegal characters, trailing dot); duplicates are compared case-insensitively because Windows folders are. pending_updates()/with_pending() let readers that must not act on stale statuses (reminder, api state) see what a locked Excel deferred. The Engagement sheet (EngagementInfo, load/write_engagement_info) carries what the old registry held; create_template() always writes it. add_any_keyword() is how a person's filing decision teaches the router. A blank Allowed Extensions loads as DEFAULT_EXTENSIONS and '*' as anything; create_template writes '*' for an item with none. check_manifest() is the app's Check Manifest button and the top of every scheduled pass: the loader's problems, plus warnings for rows the rules cannot act on. summarize() is the one count of where an engagement stands (waived outside every figure, Accepted = Received); the Unfiled sheet is no longer written. A blank Date Pattern on a row whose Period names a year derives that year's check (date_pattern_derived=True, never written back, never routing evidence - see has_routing_rules); '*' means no year check. Decision 55: check_manifest() warns when a keyword is a bare family number (FORM_FAMILIES). Decision 58: as_text() keeps a value written from data a string; an empty note replaces the old one; check_manifest() warns on a keyword with no letters or digits (EMPTY_KEYWORD_WARNING). Decision 59: atomic_replacement() never lets the temp's removal mask the write's own error; create_template() saves atomically. Decision 62: derived_date_pattern() asks for the month a Period names. Decision 66: the Engagement sheet's text cells go through as_text() too. Decision 68: with_pending() matches identifiers without case, as load_manifest() does. Decision 72: csv_tuple() takes a list or tuple as the list it already is (a spec's ["pdf"] stringified to one extension called ['pdf'], and every document parked against that row), and tracker.templates reads spec fields through it; check_tax_year() is the one bound on a tax year (YEAR_OUT_OF_RANGE), used by the wizard and the rollover alike. Decision 86: the Engagement sheet gained a Form cell and EngagementInfo a form field - which catalog the request list was cut from, as the catalog keys it. ENGAGEMENT_FIELDS owns the label and the sheet is read by label, so the cell is added after the ones already there and an engagement made before it loads with a blank; create_template() takes form as an optional keyword and folds it into the info it writes, because it is one fact about the engagement and not a property of any row - every caller that hands over rows alone records a blank, and a blank never clears a form the info already carries. Nothing refuses a manifest for a blank one. Decision 87: write_statuses() appends a scanned event and add_any_keyword() a keyword_learned event to the engagement's own record (tracker/ledger.py), each after its own write and only while locking.lock_is_held() says the caller is a pass - a request list seeded into a workbook by a test or a tool is not a pass and records nothing, and the record's own bootstrap means the first real pass imports where those rows stood anyway. Only what changed is recorded, so a pass that found the engagement as it left it appends nothing; the statuses go through _update_to_json(), the same shape the pending sidecar stores, so there is one owner for it. A deferred write records too: every reader overlays the sidecar, so which file the statuses landed in is the workaround and not the fact. Decision 88: load_manifest() now takes each identifier's Status, Received Date, File Count and Validation Notes FROM THAT RECORD wherever it has ever recorded one (_recorded_statuses(), replayed through with_pending() so there is one rule for replacing a row's scanner columns and one for matching an identifier without case), and leaves the workbook's own columns for an identifier the record has never seen - per identifier, so an engagement scanned before the record and a row added to the list since both read exactly as they always did. The request itself is never the record's: the keywords, the periods, the extensions, Waived, Manual Override and Any Keywords are the person's and always come from the workbook. load_manifest_from_workbook() is the workbook's own reading and statuses_from_workbook() its scanner columns with the pending sidecar overlaid, both public because the scanned bootstrap imports from them and the agreement fixture checks the record against them; through load_manifest() it would be checking the record against itself. A record that does not read as one is said loudly with the engagement and the line, and the workbook answers instead. Decision 89: _COLUMN_WIDTHS became COLUMN_WIDTHS - the Requests sheet is now drawn twice, here and by the view a pass regenerates, and a second copy of those numbers would drift. Decision 90: keyword_alternatives() lives here, beside csv_tuple(), because this module owns how a keyword cell is read - one keyword may name alternatives with '|' and join the phrases one of them wants together with '+', so a row can say 'these three words, or this one' where a column of ANDs and a column of ORs cannot; templates.py writes cells in that shape and content_check.py reads them, and neither owns it. Decision 93: entity_keyword() is the one normalisation for an entity's name in a keyword cell - commas, | and + become the space between words (the cell is comma-separated and | / + are the keyword grammar's) and periods are dropped so 'Ashford Holdings, L.P.' and 'Ashford Holdings LP' are one row. narrowing_rows() says which rows narrow which: a broad row that recognises its document on Any Keywords alone, and the rows that share one of those words and require something more - the shape an issuer row has. It is empty for every shipped catalog (tests/test_templates.py), so the router's issuer rule can only fire on a row a person added. check_narrowing_names() runs on every load and refuses a list where one issuer name's tokens sit inside another's, naming both rows and the row they narrow: 'Ashford' and 'Ashford Holdings' would otherwise make each other useless in silence.

tracker/scaffold.py.role: Turns a manifest into folders: Shared/ (the client's one drop folder) + Shared/PBC/, and Prepared/<folder_name_for(item)>/ plus 00 - Needs Review. Writes the client's _README.txt.
tracker/scaffold.py.notes: Also the home of the path constants every other module imports: MANIFEST_FILENAME, SHARED_DIR_NAME, PBC_DIR_NAME, PREPARED_DIR_NAME, REVIEW_DIR_NAME. Runs on every scheduled pass now; the README is rewritten only when its text changed. The README contact comes from the Engagement sheet (firm, else sender) unless given. Decision 61: the README is written whole and a failure to refresh it is a log line, never the end of a pass. Decision 89: it is still the home of the folder and manifest names, but the view's own file name lives in tracker/view.py with the module that writes it, as the index's does in tracker/filer.py and the record's in tracker/ledger.py - one owner, the writer.

tracker/validators.py.role: Tiers 1-2: does the file exist, is the extension allowed, is it big enough, is the PDF readable. Pure read-only functions plus passive cloud-placeholder detection for OneDrive and Google Drive.
tracker/validators.py.notes: Never downloads a cloud-only placeholder — a stub must never be filed as if it were the document. A file that vanishes between listing and stat is reported pending_sync, never raised — a scheduled scan must not die on one replaced file. PdfVerdictCache is a run's memo of PDF readability (the router asks once per manifest row for one file; the scanner asks again): the filer and the scanner each make one and pass it down, so nothing is shared at module level between runs that might one day be concurrent. UNFINISHED_SUFFIXES is the one list of transfer-in-progress names (decision 56).

tracker/content_check.py.role: Tier 3: extract text (pdfplumber / openpyxl / plain text, optional OCR) and test it against the row's keyword and date rules. extract() is the one reading of a document, used by the router and the scanner alike; ContentCache (CACHE_FILENAME) keeps the verdicts.
tracker/content_check.py.notes: The cache stores verdicts only - pass/fail, the reason, and the Evidence behind them, all of it the firm's own words. Extracted client text is never persisted. Only the first MAX_PAGES pages of a PDF are read, text or OCR - the identifying words are up front and a long ledger used to stall a run. Verdicts are keyed by the file's content digest and the row's rules fingerprint (CACHE_VERSION; an older layout is reset), with a per-path memo of size/mtime/digest so an unchanged file is not re-hashed: the same bytes are read twice in this system, once as a drop the router routes and once as the working copy the scanner checks, and a verdict the router reached is the verdict the scanner finds. extract(ocr=False) hands a scan back with needs_ocr set so the router can try the file's name first; extract_by_ocr() finishes the reading. The CLI (python -m tracker.content_check <engagement> <file>) prints what the document says and which rows accept it, writing no cache. The cache file is saved through manifest.write_json_atomically(), so a scan killed mid-save leaves the previous cache rather than an empty one that re-extracts everything. Decision 55: contains_keyword() treats a hyphen-joined form variant as part of the form's name (1098 never matches 1098-T); a verdict that is the machine's (no OCR, OCR failed) is transient and never cached. Decision 57: FORM_VARIANTS is the one list of each form's real variants; _JOINER is what may sit between a number and its variant or a keyword's words; the text-layer floor is per page; CACHE_VERSION 3. Decision 60: _seams() lets a keyword typed w2 find W-2; no letters or digits means no keyword. Decision 62: says() is contains_keyword() as content evidence - a form number counts only within TITLE_CHARS; _seams() reads plurals, keeps numbers out of amounts, takes any apostrophe. Decision 63: dominant_forms() - a form number counts in the text when it is in the title or is the number the document mentions most; form <anything> is a form number. Decision 64: dominant_forms() weighs a mention by its shape - a form names itself with its year or revision and another form in a sentence. Decision 66: the title is weighed the same way (_title_forms(); _REFERENCE_BEFORE marks a form quoted after attach/forms/see/of/on/and/or), a number outside FORM_VARIANTS is a mention only after Form, a keyword's words sit on one line or wrap as a heading from a line's start (_WRAPPING_JOINER, _LINE_START), a sheet's cells are tab-separated within a row; CACHE_VERSION 5. Decision 67: what comes before a form is read before what follows it (attach Form 1098 (2025) is a reference); a title naming _LIST_OF_FORMS or more forms names none; the title window is measured on the lower-cased text; _LINE_START admits a bullet, a pipe or a rule. Decision 68: _LIST_OF_FORMS counts families (_FAMILY), so a consolidated 1099 is one family's document; _REFERENCE_BEFORE stays on one line. Decision 69: a form number set off by a dash is a reference (_REFERENCE_AFTER), a dash before the year is still dated (_SELF_AFTER), and _REFERENCE_BEFORE reads across a line break again. Decision 73: says() weighs where a plain keyword is said, not only that it is there - an occurrence that is a menu line's title (_menu_tails: a form number and the title a dash or a comma sets off from it are one reference) or what an ask-word asked for (_asked_for: attach, provide, send, see and their kin, governing the rest of their own sentence and the line a request wraps on to) is the page talking about a document rather than being one, and one occurrence that is neither is enough. A dash-set-off form that heads its line with a year beside it, where the title window holds no second such line and no ask precedes it, names itself (_titles_its_own_line), so a payer's substitute form is not read as a checklist. A form number after a comma continues a list (_LIST_CONTINUES), and enclosed/enclosure/enclosures/re: join _REFERENCE_BEFORE, which now reads a colon between the word and the form. any_keyword_matched() answers the router's question 'did this row's keywords match, apart from the year?'. CACHE_VERSION 6. Decision 82: a verdict keeps the evidence behind it. Evidence(rule, term, where, page) is the one shape - EVIDENCE_RULES (required, any, date, filename, refused) and EVIDENCE_PLACES (title, first_page, footer, deep) are the named values, imported by the router, the index and the app's vocabulary and retyped nowhere. says() became a thin wrapper over _says_where(), which reaches the same verdict by the same reading and also says where the word was found (_where_said(): the title window first, then a page's last _FOOTER_LINES non-blank lines, then the rest of page 1, then deep), so no placement moved. evaluate_rules() puts an Evidence per matched rule on ContentResult.evidence, on a failing verdict too, and the reason sentence is untouched; the date rule records the row's Period, not the regex it derives and not a word of the document. format_evidence()/parse_evidence() are the one owner of the index cell's compact form (term@where:page rule, candidates joined by '; '), and the page is left off when it is 0. CACHE_VERSION 7, because a version-6 verdict read back would claim a verdict with no reason behind it. Decision 85: a form heading its own line with its printed title after its number and its year after the title names itself, at the weight a bare number-then-year mention carries - _names_itself() is the one predicate, and it holds both shapes a printed title wears (a dash between number and title, decision 69/73's; or nothing between them, _SELF_TITLED). The IRS's 2024 and 2025 W-2 revisions print one copy to the page, so Copy B's only "W-2" is the foot's "W-2 Wage and Tax Statement 2025 Department of the Treasury" and the form said nothing about itself before this. The year must be a year and not a date's tail ("Form 941 04/30/2025" on a CP 575 is a filing deadline), and a page heading two such lines is a menu, as it is for the dashed shape - _lists_forms() counts both. CACHE_VERSION 8, because a cached verdict from before it would say a one-copy W-2 is nobody's form. Decision 90: a keyword may name alternatives and join the phrases one of them wants together, read through manifest.keyword_alternatives() - says() takes the first alternative whose every phrase is said and places the evidence at its leading phrase, contains_keyword() reads a file name the same way, and a keyword holding neither character is one phrase exactly as before. CACHE_VERSION 9, because a verdict cached before it read the '|' and the '+' as words to look for.

tracker/router.py.role: Decides which single manifest row a dropped file belongs to. Evidence order: required keywords, then any-keywords/period, read off a text layer or off OCR (OCR routes on required keywords only). There is no third tier: a file name is never evidence for a filing (decision 92), and a document nothing could be read out of parks.
tracker/router.py.notes: Reads the document through content_check.extract() - the scanner's reading - and leaves its per-row verdicts in the content cache keyed by content, so the scan finds them under the working copy's name. Every scan with no text layer is OCR'd, whatever its name says, and OCR text routes only on required keywords - an any-keyword match on OCR text is OCR_ONLY, a lead for a person, because a misread word is how a document lands under the wrong request. One PdfVerdictCache per file (or the caller's) so a PDF is parsed once, not once per row. The CLI (python -m tracker.router <engagement> <files>) says where each file would go and why, moving nothing. Extension alone never routes. A document matching one row's required keywords but failing its other rules is contested and blocks its own filing — misfiling a tax document is worse than not filing it. When nothing routes, the reason is the most useful one available: a document whose content fits a row that refused the file (size floor, type, unreadable PDF) is reported as CONTESTED_PREFIX, and a file every row refused for the same reason carries that reason. A file name is read the same whole-token way a keyword is, run-together spelling and all (W2 for W-2), but only ever as evidence for a person. Eligibility is has_routing_rules(): keywords or a typed year; a year derived from Period only checks a document a keyword already matched. Decision 55, as decision 92 left it: a text layer extract() marked needs_ocr is no text at all, so a multi-page scan is read no further than a one-page one - and where 55 then filed it on its name, it now parks. Decision 58: no run-together fallback; the keyword pattern already reads a dash or space as optional. Decision 73: a row whose any-keywords all matched and whose year alone failed is remembered as a lead, and a file that would otherwise be parked with 'matched no request' is parked as 'looks like J01 (expected period not found ...)' with J01 as its candidate - the sentence a contested file gets, so the reminder asks the client about the period. A lead pre-empts no filing, unlike a required-keyword match, so the decision is exactly as it was; only the reason and the candidates improve. Decision 82: Routing.evidence_record is why, beside Routing.evidence, the tier the decision rested on - EVIDENCE_CONTENT or nothing, since decision 92 removed EVIDENCE_FILENAME (nothing rests on a name; content_check.RULE_FILENAME, the word an index row actually carries, is untouched and still produced). Keyed by candidate identifier: the content check's own Evidence tuple for a row that was read, _filename_evidence() for what the name said (a name is all title and has no page), and _refusal_evidence() for a tier-2 refusal, which travels as reasons.Reason.code rather than the sentence a person reads. _recorded_for() cuts it down to the identifiers the decision names, because every row considered leaves something behind and one index cell must not carry the whole manifest's workings. It decides nothing: every verdict is reached exactly as it was before there was a record. Decision 84: a blocked file - content fits a row, the same row's tier-2 rules refused the file - keeps the verdict's evidence beside the refusal in record, because the refusal alone says which rule said no and never which request the document looked like. The verdict was already read there to decide the file was blocked, so nothing is computed twice and no placement moves. Decision 92, the owner's (2026-09-18): A DOCUMENT NOBODY CAN READ IS FILED BY NOBODY. The by-name tier is gone - when no word of the file could be read (a scan with no text layer OCR could not rescue, an image-only PDF, an empty sheet) no row is a candidate, and the file parks with reasons.NO_READABLE_TEXT (router.UNREADABLE), which is deliberately not UNMATCHED: nothing was matched against anything, and the fix is OCR or a person, never another keyword. _filename_evidence() stays and is recorded on the parked row, so review.triage() offers the request the name points at at RULE_STRENGTH's weakest tier and the app's card and the Status Report show it - a place for a person to start reading, never a filing. _read() no longer skips OCR for a sensibly named scan: nothing is filed on a name, so OCR is the only thing that can still file one, and the scan whose name says W-2 is exactly the one whose content must be read (the _filename_hit shortcut went with the skip). The cost was stated and accepted: until Tesseract is installed every scanned PDF parks - twelve rows of the firm's own corpus moved from filing to parking, and two the name had been misfiling now park instead. Decision 93 (a row per issuer): an issuer row is an ordinary row carrying the entity's name in Required Keywords, and which row wins needed no new rule - a required keyword is the strongest tier and the generic K-1 row has none, so the issuer row takes the K-1 that names it. The one rule added is the park: when any row narrows the row that accepted a document (manifest.narrowing_rows over the rows this pass considers, so a waived issuer row is nobody's issuer) and none of the narrowing rows matched, nothing is filed - reasons.ISSUER_NOT_NAMED, the narrowing rows named, shortlist led by the row that did accept it. Filing on the generic row would put two entities' K-1s in one folder; taking the row left over would be guessing by elimination.

tracker/filer.py.role: Sorts the client's drop folder: moves each original into Shared/PBC/ untouched, copies a renamed working file into Prepared/... or 00 - Needs Review, and appends every move to _index.xlsx.
tracker/filer.py.notes: Content-hash de-duplication makes re-runs no-ops. _sort_one() decides one preserved original's fate against a _SortContext built once per run (manifest, index so far, folders, claimed names, the run's caches). The verdicts the router reaches while sorting are written to the engagement's content cache (content_check.CACHE_FILENAME, keyed by content), so the scan that follows finds them under the working copy's name and never reads the document twice; a dry run saves nothing. Originals are moved byte for byte under their own names and never altered. Each drop is handled on its own: a drop that cannot be moved is left in place for the next run, a drop that fails after it was preserved is indexed as Needs Review with the error, and the index is written in a finally block so nothing moved into PBC/ is ever unrecorded. If Excel holds _index.xlsx, the whole index as it should now read waits in _index.pending.json as a versioned snapshot (INDEX_SIDECAR_VERSION) and read_index() returns that snapshot in the workbook's place until the next write lands it; a bare-list sidecar from before the version key holds only rows to append and is folded in once. A snapshot, not a tail, because the row assign_review_file() rewrites is as much at stake as a row that was added - deferring only the rows past the workbook's end lost it while the working copy had already moved. A waiting sidecar is landed on every real run, even one whose drops were all left in place. Holds the engagement lock (tracker.locking) while it runs, so a sort and a scan never overlap - taken before the manifest, the index or the drop folder is read, so a run that finished in between is never invisible to this one. Files the client drops straight into the visible PBC/ are filed and indexed in place; a re-sent document whose working copy vanished from Prepared/ is re-filed rather than called a duplicate; a Document renamed in Excel keeps filing into the folder that already holds its files (assign_folders, not folder_name_for); empty client folders are cleared after sorting. assign_review_file() is the person's counterpart to file_drops(): moves the parked copy under the canonical name (or copies from PBC/ if it is gone), rewrites the index row as Filed with the ASSIGNED_BY_PERSON reason, learns a keyword onto the request, all under the engagement lock (the manifest read and the keyword written back included). INDEX_LAYOUT is the one description of _index.xlsx (header and width per IndexEntry field); the index is written and read back by header name, so a reordered column cannot shift a value. Decision 54: read_index() prefers a snapshot only while the workbook is older than it, keeping a snapshot-only row and a person's decision either way; write_index() never reports a landed write as deferred; replaced_in_pbc() says when an original in PBC/ no longer holds the bytes its row recorded; _existing_copy() reuses a working copy a killed run left behind; assign_review_file() rolls the move back when the index write fails for a reason other than Excel. Decision 56: replaced_in_pbc() decides by bytes alone; _copy_whole() leaves no half-written copy; the assign rollback checks _index_records() first; unfinished_drops() covers every UNFINISHED_SUFFIXES name. Decision 58: a Duplicate row never shadows the Filed row; assign_review_file() reuses a copy a killed attempt left and copies whole-or-nothing; index cells are written as text whatever they start with. Decision 59: assign refuses a replaced or still-syncing original; the rollback removes only a copy it made. Decision 61: the preserved original is hashed after the move, where it now is. Decision 65: an empty digest is nobody's duplicate. Decision 66: every move is a rename (_move_whole(); shutil.move copied a held-open drop, truncated, into PBC); assign_review_file() records the bytes of a row that has none and _record_missing_digests() does so on a later pass; what lies behind a junction is not a drop (_through_a_link()) and a junction is never rmdir'd; a name Windows cannot open is reported every pass (unreachable_drops()); the index is written with a row counter, not max_row. Decision 67: bytes recorded late are the working copy's, never the original's as it is now (_record_missing_digests(); assign refuses a replaced original by the parked copy's bytes); a name UTF-8 cannot hold is reported and never sorted (_storable(), in PBC too); write_index() retries and snapshots on any OSError; a link is a mount point or a symlink by reparse tag (_LINK_TAGS), a cloud placeholder is not one; unlistable_folders() reports a folder the run cannot list; PBC is not walked through a link; a failed rollback inside assign is logged and the write's error raised. Decision 68: a row recorded without its bytes is tied to them only while its working copy and its original agree (UNTIED_IN_PBC says the rest every pass); assign moves the parked copy only while it holds the row's bytes; a row is blank when no known column holds anything; unlistable_folders() prunes links, PBC and staging. Decision 69: _read_index_workbook() finds the header row (_MANDATORY_COLUMNS, _HEADER_WITHIN) and refuses a sheet with rows and no header; REPLACED_IN_PBC and UNTIED_IN_PBC are FileReport.attention, not errors; a parked path a later row records is the later row's (_copy_taken_by_a_later_row); assign reuses an earlier attempt's copy first and leaves an annotated parked copy, saying so (AssignResult.left_in_review); unlistable_folders() walks PBC. Decision 72: the rows above the header row are data too (a sort with 'my data has headers' unchecked puts the header last or in the middle, and everything above it was dropped in silence) - only a row with no mandatory column filled is a typed title, and a pass that found rows above the header logs how many; the index's sheet is chosen by the header, not wb.active (_sheet_with_the_header(); a renamed tab beside a person's own empty tab read as no rows and the next write rebuilt the workbook over both), and _index_workbook() rewrites only that sheet in the workbook already there, so a sheet a person added survives; a recorded original that has left PBC/ is reported every pass (missing_in_pbc(), MISSING_IN_PBC) and, where a stray carries its bytes, the row follows the file instead of a Duplicate row being written (_follow_moved_originals(), MOVED_IN_PBC; a row with no digest is never relocated); _storable() also refuses a name openpyxl cannot write (a control character, reachable on POSIX); the tidy-up (the content cache, _prune_empty_dirs()) runs on a pass with nothing to sort, and the sort loop is _sort_all(); the assign rollback puts back a parked copy a reused attempt's copy stood in for. Decision 76: dismiss_review_file() is the other thing a person may do to a parked row - it rewrites it NOT_REQUESTED with the DISMISSED_BY_PERSON reason and moves nothing at all, because a document the client sent is never deleted over a decision about the request list. _find_parked() takes a dismissed row too, so filing it is the undo and there is no second path; known (the duplicate test) already held it, so the same bytes sent again are a Duplicate rather than a second review item; _by_a_person() is the one reading of who decided a row, and read_index()'s snapshot merge keeps either decision over a workbook Excel saved stale. Decision 77: unfile_document() is the way back - the working copy returns to 00 - Needs Review under the client's own name, the row is rewritten NEEDS_REVIEW with no identifier and the UNFILED_BY_PERSON reason, and the engagement is re-scanned (outside the lock, which the scan takes for itself) so the request reverts with its regression note; the alternative people had was dragging the file in Explorer, which the index never learns. A working copy that is no longer the row's bytes is left in the request folder and said out loud (LEFT_FILED), the way assign leaves an annotated parked copy. _the_later_row() is how the snapshot merge tells which of two rows for one original was written last - the later one carries the other's whole Reason inside its own - because an unfiled row is parked again and 'the workbook still shows it parked' had stopped meaning 'before the decision'. Decision 82: IndexEntry.evidence is the last column of INDEX_LAYOUT (header Evidence), written from routing.evidence_record through content_check.format_evidence() and read back through parse_evidence() by IndexEntry.evidence_record - one owner for the cell's shape, a writer here and a reader in the app would have been two. A filed row and a parked row both carry it, and a person's decision (assign, dismiss, unfile) leaves it alone: what the rules saw is the audit trail the override was made against. _MANDATORY_COLUMNS is unchanged, so an index written before the column reads with '', and the snapshot sidecar round-trips it without a version bump (_entry_from_json() already ignores what it does not know and defaults what is missing). Decision 87: every locked write of the index is followed, in the same locked section, by the events that write added or changed, appended to the engagement's own record through tracker/ledger.py - one rule, _rows_changed(), read off the rows themselves rather than collected as the pass goes, so a drop sorted, bytes recorded on a row preserved without them, a row that followed an original the client moved and a row a person rewrote are all recorded and none can be forgotten by a later edit somewhere else. ledger_key() is the identity a row is recorded under (its PBC location) and _ledger_row() is asdict(), the shape the snapshot sidecar already writes, so row serialisation keeps one owner. Where the record already carries rows it is the record, not the pass's own reading of the index, that the new rows are compared against, so a row that reached the workbook by a road no writer took - an older bare-list sidecar folded in, a cell somebody typed over in Excel - is learned on the very next write; the person's decisions record in a finally when _index_records() says the write landed, so an interrupt between the workbook landing and the append cannot lose the one decision a person made. Decision 88: read_index() now ANSWERS FROM THAT RECORD wherever it holds an index-shaped event - the rows the writers recorded, in the index's order - and falls back to the workbook where it does not (a legacy folder, or one whose record holds nothing but a scan); every reader above it (runner, scanner, reminder, api._state, review.triage, rollover reading last year) switches with it because they all come through here and none gained a call of its own. read_index_from_workbook() is the workbook's own reading, public because the record's bootstrap imports from it, _index_records() must ask it (it is asked between a write landing and the record learning of it, and the record would say no to the write in question, rolling a person's filing back), and the agreement fixture would otherwise compare the record with itself. A record that does not read as one falls back to the workbook and says so loudly with the engagement and the line (_recorded_rows()), never a silent skip; a row a sidecar holds that the record has never seen is read, said out loud and recorded by the next write (_sidecar_rows_off_the_record()); and a workbook with rows and no header row the tracker knows is still refused before the record answers (_refuse_an_index_edited_past_reading(), the one wording shared with the workbook reading through _the_index_sheet()), because the index is still rewritten every pass. The workbook and both sidecars are written exactly as before - dropping a write is stage B. THE DELIBERATE CYCLE: _rescan() imports tracker/scanner.py at call time so a person's filing is scanned the moment it lands, and the scanner imports this module's index reader at call time; neither runs at load, the code says so beside the import, and the curated deliberate_cycle edge is the statement.

tracker/review.py.role: Triages the review queue: turns the evidence an index row kept into a ranked shortlist of at most three requests a parked file might belong to, each with the one-line reason it is on the list. Layer 2 - it suggests, and it files nothing.
tracker/review.py.notes: Decision 83. triage(engagement_dir) returns one Triage per index row decided NEEDS_REVIEW, each holding the row and a tuple of Suggestion(identifier, reason, rank). It writes no artifact at all: no sidecar, no status, no move, no lock, and no client document is opened - the index's Evidence column is already the store, and a second one could disagree with it the moment somebody filed a row by hand. It reads the manifest and the index (read_index with quarantine off, so not even an unreadable sidecar is moved aside); a caller that already loaded either passes it in. rank sorts ascending as (identity, strength, catalog): identity is a slot reserved for a later step and constant today, strength is RULE_STRENGTH before PLACE_STRENGTH so a required keyword said deep outranks an any-keyword in a title - the way the router already weighs the two rules - and the manifest's own order breaks a tie as a tie. Evidence only: the request list's Missing/Received state is deliberately not a tiebreaker and never fills a shortlist (owner, 2026-09-18), because a nudge with nothing behind it is how a tired reviewer files the wrong document into the last open row. So a row whose evidence says nothing - matched no request, a scan whose name says nothing either, a record carrying only a refusal - gets an empty shortlist and keeps the router's own reason, and a waived row is never suggested. Since decision 92 an unreadable scan whose name DOES carry a row's keyword arrives here with RULE_FILENAME evidence and is offered as 'A01 - the file name says W-2' at the bottom of the ranking: the one piece of evidence the client wrote rather than the form, so it starts a person reading and can never outrank a word the document itself said. A RULE_REFUSED entry is never a suggestion by itself; beside content evidence its cause is said in that suggestion's sentence, in the words reasons.py gives it. PLACE_WORDS is the one mapping from an evidence place to the words for it, so api._vocab() can expose it rather than the app typing a word of its own. Nothing below it imports it, and it imports neither runner, scheduling, settings nor api; genre and group are reserved for later steps.

tracker/scanner.py.role: The orchestrator: walks Prepared/, runs the three validation tiers, resolves each row's status (override- and revert-aware), and writes the result back into the manifest.
tracker/scanner.py.notes: Holds the per-engagement lock through engagement_lock() - the same context manager the filer uses - and reads the manifest only once it has it, so a sort that finished in between is never invisible to the scan. Never touches Shared/ at all. The lock itself lives in tracker.locking (ScanLockedError is an alias of EngagementLockedError). Reads each document through content_check.extract(), the same reading the router made of it as a drop, and usually finds the router's verdict already in the content cache; one PdfVerdictCache per scan. _resolve_status() is the status rule and _received_date() the Received-Date rule, named so _scan_item() reads as the three tiers and then the two decisions. A Received row whose Expected Count was raised says so instead of REGRESSION_FILES_CHANGED. An Accepted row is written Received with a date (decision 33); ScanReport.summary is the one count. No Unfiled sheet: the index records parked files; ScanReport.warnings names loose files and unrecognised folders in Prepared/, and ScanReport.summary is summarize() over the rows as the scan leaves them. Decision 54: the scan reads the manifest with_pending(), so a Received Date the last deferred scan stamped is carried, not re-stamped, and a regression is measured from the status the sidecar holds. Decision 58: a working copy the index says a person filed (ASSIGNED_BY_PERSON) is counted without the content rules (ACCEPTED_NOTE); the scan reads the index for that, and writes only the manifest. Decision 60: a person's acceptance is the newest row for the location and its recorded bytes. Decision 62: a person's filing waives tier 2 too. Imports the filer's index reader at call time; the filer imports this module at call time inside _rescan() - the deliberate cycle, stated on the filer's node.

tracker/locking.py.role: One lock per engagement (LOCK_FILENAME, O_EXCL, stale after STALE_LOCK_SECONDS), held by the filer while sorting and by the scanner while scanning. EngagementLock (the open handle and its token), EngagementLockedError; engagement_lock() context manager, taken before the manifest, index or drop folder is read.
tracker/locking.py.notes: Exists because two runs on one engagement (scheduler repeat overlapping a desktop click) raced on the same originals and the loser's index rows were overwritten. Dry runs never take it. The descriptor stays open while held (Windows then refuses to delete it, so a stale-looking lock its owner still holds is refused) and release_lock() removes the file only if it still carries this run's token. RUN_TIME_LIMIT_SECONDS is the one number for how long a scheduled pass may run: tracker.scheduling renders it as the task's ExecutionTimeLimit and STALE_LOCK_SECONDS is derived above it, so a lock is presumed dead only after Task Scheduler must have killed its owner (they were typed apart before, 3600 s against a two-hour limit). One machine per clients root: a lock file synced between two machines is not a lock. lock_status()/clear_stale_lock() back the app's lock notice: a stale lock can be cleared from the app, a fresh one is refused with how long to wait. Decision 54: pid_alive() - a lock whose owner process is gone is stale at any age, so the desktop shell's timeout kill does not block the engagement until the scheduled job's limit. Decision 56: the lock line carries host=; another host's pid is unknowable, never dead. Decision 59: a lock that cannot be deleted on release is marked RELEASED_LINE, read as an owner that is gone.

tracker/ledger.py.role: The engagement's own append-only record: one JSON object per line in LEDGER_FILENAME, appended under the engagement lock by every writer that changes the index, the snapshot sidecar, the manifest's scanner columns or the pending manifest updates, and - since decision 88 - read back by filer.read_index() and manifest.load_manifest() as the answer wherever it has one. Owns the event names (preserved, filed, parked, duplicate, assigned_by_person, dismissed_by_person, unfiled_by_person, bytes_recorded, keyword_learned, scanned, imported; drafted and migrated reserved), append() / read_events() / fold() / statuses() / head(), the file name, and the CLI's --compare check of the record against the workbooks.
tracker/ledger.py.notes: Decision 87 wrote it beside the files that already exist and had nothing read it; decision 88 is stage A step 2 - THE READERS BELIEVE IT AND FALL BACK TO THE WORKBOOKS. filer.read_index() answers from fold() wherever the record holds an index-shaped event, manifest.load_manifest() takes each identifier's scanner columns from statuses() wherever the record has recorded one, and both read the workbook for what the record has not - per row and per identifier. Both workbooks and both sidecars are still written exactly as before (dropping a write is stage B) and standing rule 2 still names the index, so deleting the record puts the reading back: that is what makes the step reversible. fold() returns rows in the index's own order, and a row that changed identity keeps the place the one it left held, because the index rewrites that row where it sits and the next write rebuilds the workbook from this fold. What makes all that safe is the autouse fixture in tests/conftest.py, which folds the record back after every test in the suite and compares it with the WORKBOOKS' own readings - read_index_from_workbook() and statuses_from_workbook(), which exist by name for exactly this, since the live readers would be the record compared with itself - row for row, field for field and now in order too. `python -m tracker.ledger <folder> --compare` is the same check for one engagement, for a person, and exits 1 on a disagreement; it imports the filer and the manifest inside the CLI block, so the module itself still imports nothing of the package but locking. Sits at the bottom beside tracker/locking.py and imports only it: the events are plain dicts, so tracker/filer.py and tracker/manifest.py each serialise their own rows with the function that already owns that shape (dataclasses.asdict for an IndexEntry, exactly as the index sidecar writes it; manifest._update_to_json for a StatusUpdate), and no cycle is created. One os.write of the whole line under O_APPEND then fsync, so a kill mid-append leaves at most a torn tail with no newline after it: read_events() ignores it and the next append() truncates it, and nothing else ever rewrites the file. O_APPEND is atomic for concurrent writers on POSIX and is not on Windows, which is why append() refuses unless locking.lock_is_held() says this process holds the engagement lock - one writer and one protocol rather than a second protocol for Windows. Not SQLite: a database file a cloud client syncs is a corrupted database file, and one database per clients root would put every client's history in one file, the opposite of the rule that an engagement folder carries everything about that engagement and nothing about anyone else's. The bootstrap is what makes an engagement already a season old agree from its first line - the first writer to append imports the index as it now stands (imported), and the first scanned event imports the manifest's statuses. Rows are keyed by the original's PBC location, the identity the snapshot merge and the app's review cards already join on; a row that followed an original the client moved carries the identity it left (was), so the fold drops the vacated one. fold() passes over an event name it does not know and read_events() refuses a bad line anywhere but the tail, so a record written by a later version still reads. The reminder writes files and takes no lock, so drafted is reserved and nothing appends it; runner and api reach the writers through the filer and the scanner and make no call of their own.

tracker/settings.py.role: The settings file beside the app (SETTINGS_FILENAME): the one place the clients root and the firm are kept. clients_root()/set_clients_root(), firm()/set_firm(); product_name() reads app/package.json productName (or ENV_PRODUCT_NAME from the shell). ENV_SETTINGS_DIR from the Electron shell says where beside-the-app is. ENV_REAL_CORPUS and real_corpus_dir() name the other folder outside the repository: the firm's own redacted documents, with the expectations file's name and columns beside them.
tracker/settings.py.notes: Replaced two roots (an env var for the app defaulting to a demo folder, a command-line path for the job) that nothing tied together. set_clients_root() refuses a folder that does not exist, so a typo cannot become an empty root the run walks for ever. The file is written through manifest.write_json_atomically(): the app and the scheduling CLI can both save it, and neither may swap the other's half-written temp into place. Decision 68: an empty root is refused - Path("") is the working folder. Decision 69: the working folder under any spelling is refused as a root. Decision 71: real_corpus_dir() answers None when the variable is unset and when what it names is not a folder, because raising would fail the suite on every machine that has no corpus, CI included; it is an environment variable rather than a setting because it belongs to a machine, never to an engagement.

tracker/reasons.py.role: Every refusal said once: for each cause, the note the scanner writes (a template), the marker the reminder recognises it by, the plain sentence the client is asked with, and whether the row is the firm's to look at.
tracker/reasons.py.notes: Replaced substrings retyped in reminder.py to recognise sentences typed in validators/content_check/scanner: rewording a producer silently changed what a client was asked. tests/test_reasons.py checks each marker is part of its own template. Decision 55: reasons_in() strips the file-name prefixes the scanner writes, so a marker is never found in a client's file name. OCR_FAILED is firm-side: ours to retry, not the client's to resend (decision 57). Decision 92 added NO_READABLE_TEXT (code 'unreadable', marker 'nothing in this file could be read'), which is the ONE reason here that is not a validation note: the router writes it into the index's Reason column when no word of a file could be read, and it is firm-side because the client's document may be perfectly good and only this machine cannot read it. It is in ALL, so find() and the review card's refusal words reach it like any other. Decision 93 added ISSUER_NOT_NAMED (code 'issuer-not-named', marker 'names none of them'), the second reason here that is not a validation note: the router writes it into the index's Reason column when a request list asks for a document one row per issuer and the document names none of them. Firm-side - the client sent the right document; a person files it or adds the row.

tracker/rollover.py.role: Builds a returning client's next-year request list from their prior engagement. Prior-year data always wins; the template may only fill blanks.
tracker/rollover.py.notes: Years shift as a set so relative periods stay right. Counts learn from what arrived and never shrink. Waived carries forward; Accepted does not. The CLI's form template comes from tracker.templates, so this module and tracker.api no longer import each other. Derived year checks are left blank in the new manifest; the shifted Period derives them again. Decision 56: reads the prior year's manifest with_pending(), quarantining nothing. Decision 61: every Carried Forward cell is text. Decision 67: a template row is the prior's row whatever its case (load_manifest() compares identifiers without it); the Carried Forward widths are set by column letter. Decision 69: roll_forward() refuses a target year not after the prior's. Decision 72: and one outside YEAR_MIN..YEAR_MAX, through manifest.check_tax_year(), as the wizard's box does. Decision 86: carry_engagement_info() carries the Engagement sheet's Form cell into next year's workbook - a returning client files the same return, and the rolled list is last year's list - and carries a blank as a blank, guessing no catalog for a prior that never recorded one.

tracker/reminder.py.role: Drafts the client chase email from a scanned manifest. Draft only — there is no SMTP anywhere in this module.
tracker/reminder.py.notes: Validation notes are translated into plain client instructions, never quoted. Rows we have not read yet, and rows with no request folder, are held back for a person instead of being asked for. Each draft carries a fingerprint of its own text so an edited draft is never overwritten. A Partial row whose shortfall is a file we have not read is held back too. Overlays pending_updates() from the manifest sidecar before triaging, so a scan that Excel kept from writing still stops the draft asking for a document that arrived. Reads the Engagement sheet itself for client, link, due, sender and firm; keyword arguments are one-off overrides for the CLI. Decision 57: write_draft() raises DraftsEditedError rather than overwrite an edited NEW draft; the runner reports BOTH_DRAFTS_EDITED and writes nothing. Decision 62: EXTENSION_ASK names the row's own file types; --write preserves edits. Decision 76: count_needs_review() is still the folder's count (a file dragged in by hand has no row and is nobody's decision yet) less the working copies whose newest index row is filer.NOT_REQUESTED - the warning is there for documents nobody has looked at, and a person has looked at those. An index it cannot read leaves every file counted.

tracker/registry.py.role: Finds every engagement under the clients root: any folder holding _manifest.xlsx, without descending into one. Reads each manifest's Engagement sheet for client, link, due, sender, firm, reminders and active. There is no registry file.
tracker/registry.py.notes: Replaced engagements.yaml (decision 27): a hand-kept list a typo could silently skip a client from. Hidden/underscore folders and Prepared/Shared are skipped, depth is capped at MAX_DEPTH, an unreadable manifest is listed with its problem rather than dropped, and a root with no manifest at all is an error - that is a typo in the scheduled task, not an empty practice. mark_superseded(): an engagement another one was rolled forward from is inactive with its successor named - the rollover never writes to the prior, so the successor's sheet is the record. Engagement wraps EngagementInfo (the sheet as loaded) and delegates its fields rather than copying them, so a field added to the sheet reaches discovery without a second edit. Decision 66: _same_folder() matches Rolled From by the client and engagement folder names when the absolute path no longer resolves, so a clients root that moved does not bring retired priors back. Decision 67: _prior_of() never compares an engagement with itself and matches the engagement sharing the most trailing names (at least _TAIL_NAMES) only when it is the only one - a year level above the client has two sharing the last two; _walk_engagements() lists a folder it could not read as a problem row, never a silence. Decision 68: a Rolled From that matches nothing is a warning the engagement carries (ROLLED_FROM_UNMATCHED) and the run shows; a problem row is never the prior.

tracker/runner.py.role: The unattended pass: for every engagement in the registry, file -> scan -> (on DRAFT_WEEKDAY) draft. This is the whole scheduled task.
tracker/runner.py.notes: Owns the draft-day rule (DRAFT_WEEKDAY) in is_draft_day(); the scheduler does not know about it. One engagement's failure never stops the others, and the run exits non-zero so the scheduler shows red. A drop the filer could not sort marks the engagement failed (exit non-zero) after the scan and draft still ran. The CLI takes the clients root, not a file; an engagement whose manifest could not be read fails alone with the reason. Runs check_manifest() before touching files: problems fail the engagement with the row, warnings ride the report. Scaffolds each engagement before filing (a row added in Excel gets its folder), leaves waived rows out of the outstanding count, and skips an engagement whose successor names it in Rolled From. run_engagement() is the one definition of a pass; the app's scan command calls it too (_worth_a_pass() is its pre-checks, _draft_step() its draft). main(argv) is the command line as a function: python -m tracker.runner and the packaged executable in runner mode (api_entry.py, RUNNER_MODE_FLAG) both call it. Decision 55: should_draft() catches up a draft day the machine missed (last_drafted() from the draft files); an engagement never drafted waits for its first draft day. Decision 57/60: a quiet draft day refreshes the run's own unedited draft (_refresh_stale_draft()) so it is neither stale nor a missed week. Decision 58, as decision 60 settled it: on a quiet draft day the run's own unedited draft is rewritten by _refresh_stale_draft() and one a person has edited is never touched (the earlier rule that retired the draft is gone with its function). Decision 67: main() reconfigures stdout and stderr to replace what the console cannot encode, so a client's file name never turns a finished run into a traceback. Decision 68: append_log() replaces what UTF-8 cannot encode; an engagement's registry warning rides the run's warnings. Decision 69: a FileReport's attention rides the run's warnings, never its error. Decision 75: every real pass ends by writing STATUS_PAGE_FILENAME into the clients root, never on a dry run - the practice on one page, drawn from a report rather than from a fresh pass. status_report() folds the runs just made into every engagement the registry found and reads the rest (manifest and sidecar, no lock, nothing written), so --only and the app's one-engagement pass still draw the whole practice; write_status_page() escapes every value, fetches nothing and takes no lock, and reads each engagement's index for the review queue. skipped_because() is the one wording of why an engagement is passed over, shared with _worth_a_pass(); EngagementRun.last_pass is None on a row the page read rather than ran. Decision 87: the pass gained no call of its own on tracker/ledger.py - run_engagement() takes no lock (file_drops() and scan_engagement() each take their own) and has no run identifier, so what the pass did is recorded by the writers it calls, once per decision, and a second call here would be a second record of the same one. Decision 89: the last thing each engagement's pass does is _view_step(), which regenerates its read-only view (tracker/view.py). It follows the status page rather than the writers - drawn from what the readers now say, no lock, never on a dry run, and never able to fail a pass - and a view whose replace did not land leaves run.view_stale set (VIEW_NOT_REGENERATED in the summary line) on a run that still succeeds, because the view holds no fact of its own. Decision 91: write_status_page() is drawn through tracker/page.py - esc(), the table builder and page_text() live there now, shared with the engagement's own page, so neither can grow a second escaper. The page itself is unchanged except that its tables gained thead/tbody from that builder.

tracker/scheduling.py.role: Generates the Windows Task Scheduler XML or n8n workflow that runs tracker.runner unattended.
tracker/scheduling.py.notes: One daily task is enough because the runner decides the drafting day. Recognizes Windows drive-letter paths as absolute even when generating from Linux. Generates for a clients root (--root), not a registry file. install_task() registers the XML with schtasks (/f, so re-running changes the schedule); --install does both steps. --root defaults to the settings file's root. The task name is the product name from settings.product_name(); the defaults (start, repeat, XML file name) are module constants the API's install-schedule reports back so the app shows what was actually installed. EXECUTION_TIME_LIMIT is locking.RUN_TIME_LIMIT_SECONDS rendered by iso_duration(), not a second number, because the lock's stale threshold is derived from the same limit. runner_arguments(frozen=True) is the packaged form of the one command line: the app's executable in runner mode (runner.RUNNER_MODE_FLAG) instead of -m tracker.runner, same arguments after it. TASK_NAME at import is safe because only the shell-launched API (or a source checkout) imports this module; the frozen job never does. Decision 55: quote_argument() doubles a trailing backslash so a drive-root clients folder survives the Windows argument parser.

tracker/api.py.role: The JSON command layer the desktop app talks to; COMMANDS is the list, and the module docstring is pinned to it.
tracker/api.py.notes: Every command prints one JSON object and returns an exit code — errors are JSON too, never a traceback. This is the only module the Electron app knows about. The create path validates identifiers and counts with the same sentences the manifest loader uses, and never leaves a half-built engagement folder behind. state overlays deferred statuses and reports pending_statuses; an engagement name with nothing alphanumeric left after sanitizing falls back to a default. list/priors use the same discovery as the scheduled run; create and rollover write the Engagement sheet from the wizard's client/link/due (rollover carries client, sender, firm and reminders, never last year's link or due); assign files a parked document by a person's choice and re-scans. check validates the manifest on demand; unlock clears a stale lock; state carries the lock; templates carries each form's tax year and create names a new-client engagement from client, year and form when no name is given. create takes the tax year (calendar default) and shifts catalog rows to it; rollover writes Rolled From so the prior retires; priors report superseded_by. scan is run_engagement() with reminders=REMINDERS_NEVER - the app's button and the scheduled job make the same pass; state carries summarize(). The clients root comes from tracker.settings (settings, set-root, install-schedule commands); the wizard never writes Engagement Name, and reads the firm from settings.firm(). install-schedule works in the packaged app too: frozen, it registers its own executable in runner mode (working folder = the executable's) and reports frozen=True; from source it registers the Python it runs under. ENGAGEMENT_FLAG with nothing after it, or an empty folder, gets the same sentence as no flag; once a root is set the folder must lie under it. assign takes the lock twice on purpose (file, then re-scan), each step whole under its own lock. _vocab() hands the renderer every word it shows for a status, decision or reason - the app carries no Python vocabulary of its own. NAME_PATTERN / ROLLOVER_NAME_PATTERN are the only two engagement-name shapes. Decision 55: _under_root() checks containment whenever a root is set and for a rollover's prior too. Decision 67: a blank name falls back to the client's name sanitised, and _new_engagement_dir() refuses a name that is not a folder straight under the root. Decision 68: _tax_year() bounds the year on create and rollover alike. Decision 72: it bounds it through manifest.check_tax_year(), which the rollover's own flag now goes through too. Decision 75: a pass made from the app is on the record the scheduled run leaves - _record_pass() appends runner.append_log()'s line to the run log and redraws the status page from every engagement under the root, neither taking a lock nor being allowed to fail the pass that has already moved the files - and state reports the page's path, so the shell will open it for the app's Open Status button. Decision 76: dismiss records that no request asks for a parked document and does not re-scan - nothing was filed under a request, so no row's status can have changed. _vocab() carries the new decision under the key 'dismissed', not the word: the renderer may not hold the word 'Requested' in any form (it is manifest.UNSCANNED_LABEL, and the guard that keeps the app from typing a status reads the whole file), and review_labels carries the card's own labels so the renderer types none of them. Decision 77: unfile sends one filed document back for review and returns the rewritten row and state; the scan summary is state's, because summarize() over the rows the re-scan left has one home and a second copy in the payload would be a second answer. The re-scan itself belongs to filer.unfile_document(), not here: the status reverting is part of the correction, not part of being asked over JSON. Decision 82: state's index rows carry evidence as data, not as text - _evidence_payload() parses the cell with content_check.parse_evidence() and ships a record keyed by candidate identifier, so the renderer never splits a string of the tracker's on separators of its own; _vocab()['evidence'] carries EVIDENCE_RULES and EVIDENCE_PLACES, the two lists of words the app may label. Decision 84: state carries 'review' - tracker.review.triage() over the manifest rows and index entries state has already loaded, so each is read once for the whole screen, serialised by _triage_payload() as one entry per parked file joined to its index row by pbc_location, its shortlist in triage order, each suggestion carrying identifier, reason and rank. The reason ships whole, with its leading identifier, exactly as review.py wrote it: one owner for the sentence, and the identifier travels beside it as data because that is what assign is given. There is no review command - the card draws from the one state the app already reads. _vocab() owns every word that card shows: review_labels gained FILE_LABEL, SUGGESTED_HEADING and OTHER_REQUESTS_HEADING, and 'triage' carries review.NOTHING_SUGGESTED, review.IDENTIFIER_SEPARATOR, review.PLACE_WORDS and review.MAX_SUGGESTIONS from the module that owns them. Decision 86: create passes the wizard's catalog choice to create_template(form=...) so the Engagement sheet records which checklist the list was cut from, and _state() ships it with the rest of the sheet (_info_payload() is asdict() over EngagementInfo, so a field added there travels without a second edit). The app prints it beside the engagement picker exactly as the catalog keys it, so _vocab() gains no word for it. Decision 89: _state() ships view: {state, path} from tracker.view.view_state() - a read that takes no lock and tolerates another program holding the file - and paths gains 'view', because the shell opens only the paths this map names. _vocab() owns the label and the three state words; the app types none of them. Decision 91: paths['view'] is now an .html file, which shell.openPath() opens in the default browser by its extension, and _vocab()['view'] gained 'open', the button's own label (tracker.view.VIEW_OPEN_LABEL), so the renderer types neither word. _slug is tracker.page.slug, one function for a status chip's class in the app and a status badge's on the page.

tracker/templates.py.role: The per-form request catalog (FORM_TYPES, FORM_TEMPLATES): what each return type asks for and the keyword rules that recognise each document. The ONLY source of truth for the checklists; the wizard and the rollover read it directly.
tracker/templates.py.notes: item_from_spec() gives a rule-less request its own document name as the required keyword, because a request with no rule can never auto-file, and the safe extension default. default_tax_year() is the calendar's most recently ended year; template_items(form, year=...) shifts the catalog's base year to it, relative periods included. No date_pattern in the catalog: each row's Period implies its year check. Decision 60: a catalog keyword is the form's own title or a phrase only it carries, never a word other forms print about it (a 1040 says W-2; a 1095-C says Marketplace). Decision 62: every catalog row keys on the document's own title phrase; tests/test_catalog.py routes reconstructions of the real forms against every catalog. Decision 63: the prior-year return rows require their form number and title, so a return wins over its schedules' lines. Decision 64: the return rows require their title phrase, not their number; the K-1 row keys on the K-1's title; tests/irs/ (the IRS's own forms) and tests/test_irs_forms.py route them all. Decision 65: every prior-year return row requires the jurat; schedule rows key on their titles, not on account names. Decision 66: no row keys on a line every return prints (dividends and distributions, ownership percentage, donation) or the organizer asks (child care provider); the receipt, list and childcare rows key on those documents' own titles. Decision 67: the receipt row does not key on contribution statement (an IRA's, a 529's); the childcare row knows the provider's statement; the estimated tax row keys on a voucher's own lines (its numbered heading, the amount line), not the booklet's prose. Decision 68: the receipt row keys on receipt wording only (a pledge, a thank-you and the firm's letter are not receipts); the estimated tax row knows the state voucher; the childcare row does not take an FSA administrator's statement. Decision 69: the receipt row keys on words only a charity prints; no form 540-es; L01 has no tuition statement (a checklist's line, a university's bill). Decision 72: item_from_spec() reads a spec's lists through manifest.csv_tuple(), the one parser, rather than a copy of it. Decision 73: the shared estimated-tax row is two rows, because an individual's 1040-ES voucher is not a corporation's record (business_estimated_tax keys on corporation estimated tax, estimated tax voucher, estimated payments made); the December bank row does not key on statement of account (a credit-card issuer's and a broker's heading) and takes a workbook, as the reconciliation it asks for arrives; the property tax row keys on the bill's own titles, not on assessor, parcel number or property tax bill (an assessor's notice and a servicer's escrow analysis print those); D01 drops thank you for your donation (every fundraiser's salutation); I01 drops advance payment of premium tax credit (a marketplace notice's sentence); J01 keys on child care/day care spellings with the run-together copies deleted, since the matcher reads the space as optional; 1041 A01 names the kind of trust (an IRA custodian's paperwork is a Trust Agreement too), B02 drops year-end account statement (a bank's heading), C01 drops distribution schedule (a mutual fund's), E01 knows stepped-up basis; 990 C02 keys on the schedule's own title rather than compensation of officers (Part VII's line and the Statement of Functional Expenses', which is now a financial statement's title), D02 on grants made rather than a bare grantee (a letter the charity received) or grants paid (the 990-PF's line 25), E01 without program description (a grant proposal's); the xlsx-only rows and the loans row take the format a client really sends, and officer_comp drops form 1125-e with it (the blank IRS form parks). Decision 85: 1040 E01 knows the wording a broker actually exports - realized gain/loss and the run-together realized gain loss beside the firm's own realized gain and loss - and takes a workbook, since that export arrives as an .xlsx as often as a CSV; 1041 B01 takes the same two, because the trust's realized gain/loss export is its 1099-B by another name. No IRS form in tests/irs/ says either word, and decision 68's consolidated 1099 never prints them, so the composite's placements are untouched. Decision 90, the owner's catalog: _prior_return() writes every prior-year return row's required keyword, with JURAT as the one owner of the line decision 65 added, and a state return's own printed title as an alternative inside that keyword - a standalone CA 540 or NY IT-201 files 1040 B01 on 'resident income tax return', a CA 568 or NY IT-204 files 1065 A01 on 'return of income' or 'partnership return', a CA 100S files 1120S A01 on 'franchise or income tax return', and another state is one more phrase, not a rule. The alternative lives inside the required keyword rather than in Any Keywords so the row's required set stays required: the prior-year return still outranks a row that matched on any keyword and one that fails another rule is still contested. The 1040 catalog gains A03-A06, one row per 1099 a person receives, keyed on the form's number - 'nonemployee compensation' is said by the IRS Attention page ahead of every information return and 'certain government payments' by the 1040-ES package, so neither is a keyword; 'miscellaneous information' and 'payment card' are, the second because the 1099-K's title never lands on one line and 'payment card' begins it, where a checklist's menu rule can see it. 'depreciation' joins SHARED - the 1120's C02 unchanged, 1120S F02 and 1065 D02 new - so the schedule behind Form 4562 has one set of words; a fixed-asset register that never says depreciation stays on fixed_assets, which all three catalogs already carry. Decision 93: the catalog keeps ONE K-1 row (1040 F01, K1_CATALOG/K1_IDENTIFIER) and it asks for the state K-1 too - California heads Schedule K-1 (568) "Member's Share of Income" - because which partnerships a client is in is a fact about that client, not about the 1040. issuer_row() cuts a row per issuing entity from k1_row(): same Any Keywords, same period and extensions, the normalised entity name in Required Keywords and in the Document. The 1065's F01 is Special Allocation Support and decision 85's F1 stays open there.

tracker/__init__.py.role: Package docstring listing every component, and the re-exports of the manifest and scaffold APIs.
tracker/__init__.py.notes: Imports tracker.manifest and tracker.scaffold at load time, and tracker/manifest.py imports `from tracker import ledger`, which executes this package while it is still initialising. That is the one load-time cycle in the package, and it holds only because tracker/ledger.py imports nothing of the package but tracker/locking.py - keep it at the bottom. Every other cycle the derived edges show closes through an import at call time (the map labels those separately), and tracker/filer.py <-> tracker/scanner.py inside _rescan() is the deliberate one.

api_entry.py.role: PyInstaller entry point: the portable app's one executable, which is the tracker API by default and the scheduled job (tracker.runner.main) when RUNNER_MODE_FLAG comes first.
api_entry.py.notes: PyInstaller needs a real script, not a -m module. Runner mode is dispatched before tracker.api is imported, because the API imports tracker.scheduling whose TASK_NAME needs the product name the Electron shell passes in the environment - and Task Scheduler passes nothing; the job needs neither of the shell's variables. api_entry.spec (committed; reads config.apiName from app/package.json) is how it is frozen.

.github/workflows/ci.yml.role: CI: runs the test suite, `repo_map.py check`, the vocabulary check, the linter and `node --check` on the three Electron files, on Linux and Windows and on two interpreters, on every push to main and every pull request.
.github/workflows/ci.yml.notes: The map check is the point. docs/repo-map.md is what agents read instead of re-scanning, its freshness is guarded by test_the_committed_map_is_current, and this workflow is what makes that guard run without anyone remembering to. Every step always reports, so a stale map and a failing test surface in the same run. Windows is in the matrix because the firm's machine is Windows and the held lock, the atomic replace and the Windows-only tests behave differently there; the python-version line is pinned to pyproject's floor by a guard. Decision 78: the matrix carries the interpreter the office runs beside that floor, because the package is frozen on the office's Python and a suite that has never run there proves nothing about it; the four rows are written out one at a time rather than crossed so the floor stays one readable literal for the guard that pins it.

.github/workflows/build.yml.role: Builds the portable package on demand (workflow_dispatch or a `v*` tag) by running Build App.bat itself on a Windows runner, proves the frozen executable answers in both of its modes, prints the build-info file and uploads the package as the run's artifact for seven days.
.github/workflows/build.yml.notes: Decision 78. It runs the batch file rather than re-implementing the build, because a second copy of the build is the one that drifts; tests/test_build.py refuses a workflow that names PyInstaller, the packager or the copy itself. The batch file pauses for a person at every exit, so it reads one documented switch that skips the waits, named in its own header and set here. The two smoke checks run the frozen executable, not the source: `list` with the shell's two environment variables set, which must answer JSON rather than a traceback on an install with no clients root yet, and one dry pass over a scratch clients root tests/samples.py builds, which walks filing, routing, scanning and drafting. Where the package landed is read back out of the batch file's own OUT/PLATFORM/ARCH and app/package.json's two names, so no path here is a second copy of one. Not on push: a freeze, an npm install, an Electron download and a few hundred megabytes of artifact are not what a commit should cost.

CLAUDE.md.role: Agent entry point. Says to read the map instead of re-scanning, how to keep it current, and the standing rules that hold across every module.
CLAUDE.md.notes: Points at docs/repo-map.md as the first thing to read in a session.

docs/repo-map.curated.json.role: The hand-written half of this map: roles, notes, artifacts, cross-language hops and the standing rules. Merged on top of the derived facts and never overwritten by a rebuild.
docs/repo-map.curated.json.notes: Edit this, then run `python tools/repo_map.py update`. The generated docs/repo-map.json and docs/repo-map.md are NOT edited by hand.

tests/test_repo_map.py.role: Guards the map's trust contract: derived facts come from source, curated judgment survives regeneration, drift is detected, and the committed map matches the tree.
tests/test_repo_map.py.notes: test_the_committed_map_is_current fails the suite if someone changed code without running `repo_map.py update`.

conftest.py.role: Puts the repo root on sys.path so tests can `import tracker` without installing the package - explicitly now, beside pyproject's pythonpath, for editor runners and pytest's rootdir detection.

tools/repo_map.py.role: Builds and incrementally updates this map. Derives imports, exports, CLIs, test coverage and hashes from source; merges the curated layer on top.
tools/repo_map.py.notes: Standard library only. `update` re-parses only files whose SHA-256 changed, and a change to this file forces a full rebuild — new derivation rules must not leave edges typed by the old ones. Test edges are three-way on purpose: `tests` (the test file owning the module by name) is coverage, `exercises` (any other test importing it) is not, and a test importing another test is a plain `imports`.

tools/vocab_report.py.role: Generates the vocabulary coverage report: which keyword in each catalog is reached by which IRS form in tests/irs/ or case in tests/test_catalog.py, tested with content_check.says() the way the router reads, and which keywords nothing in the suite defends.
tools/vocab_report.py.notes: The map's counterpart for the routing rules (decision 70). `build` extracts the corpus and routes every keyword (about thirty seconds); `check` compares the SHA-256 of its inputs - the catalog, the matcher, the loader, the cases, the corpus, tests/test_real_corpus.py and this file - so it costs nothing and CI runs it. The committed report reads no client document: the corpus is the IRS's own blank forms and text the suite typed. Decision 71: when TRACKER_REAL_CORPUS names the firm's own redacted documents, `build` reads those too (kind `real`, the harness's expectations giving each one's placement) and the counts name them; that report is a local reading, never the committed one, and `check` refuses a committed report that names them. Decision 73: the workbook cases are read too - as_a_sheet() renders a sheet's rows the way content_check._extract_xlsx does, so a keyword only a schedule reaches is not reported as unreached.

tools/backtest.py.role: Routes the firm's own already-sorted documents at the office and scores the router against them: the agreement with where a person filed each one, the confusion pairs, the per-row table, the parked and no-text shares, and the time a real pass takes.
tools/backtest.py.notes: Decision 74. The measure the fifty blank IRS forms and the typed cases cannot be - decision 70's report leaves most keywords and most rows defended by nothing - and the only corpus made of documents a client actually sent. Each document is routed through a hard link (a copy where the file system refuses one) under one neutral name, so the router's by-name fallback can never read the client's name off the file and the score is the routing rules' rather than the firm's naming discipline; the link is the same bytes, so every tier-2 check still sees the real document. A document with no text layer is its own category, because the only evidence left for it would be the name being hidden - unless OCR is allowed, when nothing is handed over and the router does its own reading under its own stricter rule for OCR words. Catalogs are built the way tests/test_irs_forms.py builds them, with the size floor and the year check lifted. Nothing identifying comes back: counts, catalog identifiers and a row's number in the expectations file, never a file name, a folder name below the corpus root or a word of a document; the corpus, its expectations file and the report stay outside the repository and the tool refuses to write into the tree.

docs/backtest-baseline.json.role: The one number the backtest commits: how often the router filed the firm's own sorted documents where a person filed them, the count it was measured over, and the day it was measured.
docs/backtest-baseline.json.notes: Decision 74. Owned by tools/backtest.py; `record` writes it and `check` fails a report below it. It ships with no agreement recorded, and `check` then says plainly that the owner has not yet run the backtest at the office and exits 0 - an unknown baseline is never reported as a met one. It holds a number and a date and nothing a client could be read out of.
