tests/test_backtest.py.role: Guards the backtest: a document is routed by its text and never by its name, a file with no text layer is counted apart rather than parked, the report and the console carry no file or folder name, the skeleton is blank with the request folder as the hint and is never overwritten, and an unrecorded baseline is said rather than passed.
tests/test_backtest.py.notes: Decision 74. The corpus it scores is built with tests/samples.py in a temporary folder, because no client document is in the repository or ever will be. It also pins the two things the hiding rests on: the neutral name reaches no keyword in any shipped catalog, and a whole pass writes nothing under the repository root.

tools/learned_keywords.py.role: Lists what the staff taught the router: every keyword a person typed into one engagement's manifest that no catalog row with the same identifier and document carries, across every engagement under the clients root, grouped by request row with the number of engagements that typed it.
tools/learned_keywords.py.notes: Decision 79. A keyword learned through manifest.add_any_keyword() lives in that one manifest, so fifty engagements hold fifty private vocabularies and the catalog is the only one tests/test_catalog.py and tests/test_irs_forms.py defend; this is the season's list of candidates to promote. Read-only in the strong sense: no lock is taken, no manifest is written, the readers' quarantine=False is passed so looking never moves a sidecar, and a report path inside the repository is refused - an engagement folder name is a client's name and the report names them on request. The Engagement sheet has recorded the catalog form since decision 86, but this tool does not read it: a row is compared against every catalog holding it and the report says which matched; a row no catalog holds is a custom request, listed apart with all its keywords. An engagement whose manifest could not be read is a problem line, never a silent skip. It borrows shipped_catalogs() and corpus_documents() from tools/vocab_report.py, so the catalogs it compares against and the corpus a candidate can be run over are the coverage report's.

tests/test_learned_keywords.py.role: Guards the learned-keyword report: two engagements that taught one keyword are one row with a count of two, a keyword the catalog already carries is not reported, a hand-added row is a custom row, an unreadable manifest is a problem line, the default output holds no folder name, nothing under the repository is written and a path inside it is refused, and a keyword an IRS form says is marked as one that would misfile it.
tests/test_learned_keywords.py.notes: Decision 79. The clients roots are scratch trees under tmp_path, built the way tests/test_registry.py builds one: create_template() writes the shipped catalog and add_any_keyword() teaches the keyword, so what the report compares is a real manifest rather than a stand-in. The corpus case reads the fifty IRS forms and takes about half a minute.

tests/test_real_corpus.py.role: The harness for the firm's own redacted documents: every row of the expectations file beside them routed against a shipped catalog the way tests/test_irs_forms.py routes the IRS's forms, and asserted to file where the firm says or to park.
tests/test_real_corpus.py.notes: Decision 71. The corpus is outside the repository, in the folder TRACKER_REAL_CORPUS names, and is never committed; with no corpus the routing case skips by name and the harness's own tests - the reading, the routing and the skip - still run on a scratch folder, so the file is exercised on every machine. It owns read_expectations() and real_corpus(), which tools/vocab_report.py imports, so the report and the test cannot disagree about what an expectation means. Decision 74: read_expectations() takes the file's path rather than its folder, because tools/backtest.py scores an expectations file a person keeps wherever they keep it and the contract has to have one reader.

tests/test_vocab_report.py.role: Guards the coverage report: reach is says(), not a substring; the four headline lists are computed as claimed on small catalogs; the committed report matches its inputs by hash.
tests/test_vocab_report.py.notes: test_the_committed_report_is_current fails the suite if a keyword, a case or the matcher changed without `python tools/vocab_report.py build`. Decision 73: a workbook case must read the same to the report as to the suite, so the rendering and a real round trip through openpyxl are asserted equal.

tests/samples.py.role: The pile of client documents the suite starts from, built from nothing: text_pdf() prints lines to a real one-page PDF, sheet_xlsx() writes rows to a real workbook, and build_samples() assembles the drop folder a client would leave (a duplicate, last year's form, a Word file, a Google Sheets shortcut, a photo, a half-uploaded temp file).
tests/samples.py.notes: No fixture files in the repository and no client data, so every test starts from the same pile. It was the marketing demo's sample builder in tracker/api.py; the demo went (decision 41) and the suite still needed the pile. listing_denied() makes a folder really unlistable for the running account, because rglob and os.walk reach the file system by different calls and a monkeypatch of one proves nothing about the other. Decision 73: sheet_xlsx() is how tests/test_catalog.py routes its workbook cases - half of every catalog asks for a schedule a client keeps in Excel, and a sheet is read as rows of tab-separated cells (a phrase across two cells is one phrase, a phrase down two rows is two labels), so typing one as prose would prove the wrong reading. Decision 78: build_scratch_root() assembles the same pile into a whole clients root - one scaffolded engagement with the documents already dropped - which is what .github/workflows/build.yml runs the frozen package over; the fixture lives beside the pile rather than in a tool of its own so there is one pile and not two that drift.

tests/test_build.py.role: Guards what only the build workflow could otherwise discover ten minutes into a release: that it runs the batch file the repository owns rather than a copy of the build, that the switch it sets is the one that batch file reads, that the flags it fires at the frozen executable are flags tracker/runner.py declares, that it passes the two environment variables tracker/settings.py names, and that both workflows quote the one interpreter pyproject.toml writes down.
tests/test_build.py.notes: Decision 78. It also asserts the fixture: a scratch root is one engagement discovery finds and a whole dry pass walks, because a smoke check over an empty folder proves only that discovery does not crash. Nothing here can prove the package runs - only the Windows runner can.

docs/vocab-coverage.md.role: The vocabulary coverage report as people read it: the unreached keywords, the keywords reached only by documents that file elsewhere, the rows nothing files into, then every catalog row by row. Generated by tools/vocab_report.py; never edited by hand.
docs/vocab-coverage.md.notes: Rebuilt with `python tools/vocab_report.py build` in the same commit as a catalog, matcher or case change.

docs/vocab-coverage.json.role: The coverage report as data, with the SHA-256 of every input it was built from; `check` and the suite compare against these. Generated; never edited by hand.

app/main.js.role: Electron main process. Spawns the Python API (`python -m tracker.api`, or the frozen executable package.json's config.apiName names in the portable build) and relays its JSON to the renderer over IPC.
app/main.js.notes: This is the cross-language boundary: everything the UI can do is a tracker.api command. The renderer is untrusted here: a command must be in vocab.commands (before the vocabulary arrives, only BOOTSTRAP_COMMAND, pinned to tracker.api.COMMANDS by a guard) with the one argument shape the renderer uses; open-path opens only a path the API reported in state.paths; the tracker's exit code is read, not discarded, and a tracker that outlives TRACKER_TIMEOUT_MS is killed and reported. The window is sandboxed, cannot navigate and cannot open windows.

app/preload.js.role: Context bridge exposing only the calls tests/test_single_source.py checks against main.js.call(args, payload), tracker.open(path) and tracker.pickFolder(). Nothing else crosses.

app/renderer/app.js.role: The desktop UI: the form-type wizard, the request list and the scan results. Talks only to window.tracker from the preload bridge.
app/renderer/app.js.notes: Every node is built with el() and placed with replaceChildren; there is no innerHTML and no escaper, so a client's file name, a note typed in Excel or a folder name is text whatever characters it carries (a guard checks the sinks are absent). Every word it shows or compares comes from the API's vocabulary (applyVocabulary); SCAN_LABEL is the one label it owns. Decision 76: the Needs Review card asks one question of a parked and a set-aside document alike - which request does this belong to - so reviewRow() builds both, and only an open question carries the note box and the button that sets one aside; what a person has set aside is folded under its own count, never removed from the page, because the list is the only way back. Decision 77: renderUnfileList() is the same list for what is already filed - folded away, there for the one row that is wrong - and the function cannot be called after the decision it shows, because the guard on the renderer's vocabulary forbids that word anywhere in the file. Decision 84: the Needs Review card shows the shortlist. renderReview() maps state.review by pbc_location and hands each parked row its triage; reviewRow() puts the shortlist at the head of the picker under the 'suggested' heading, every other request under 'other_requests', and lists the sentence behind each suggestion beneath the row - an <option> carries no second line, and the reason is what is read before anything is picked. The picker starts on the best suggestion, falling back to the router's own first candidate. A parked file the evidence says nothing about shows the vocabulary's nothing_suggested rather than a guess, and a set-aside row is not triaged at all, so it gets no shortlist. Every word of it - the two headings and the File it label as well - comes from vocab; the renderer still types none. Decision 89: a chip beside the engagement's name says whether its own page still describes it. The word and the label are the API's (vocab.view), the chip's class is derived from the word the same way a status chip's is, and the button opens state.paths.view through the same whitelisted opener the Open Status button uses. Decision 91: that button's label is the API's too - applyVocabulary() fills #view-label from vocab.view.open, exactly as it fills the scan button - so the page carries no word for it, and the path it opens is now an .html file the shell hands to the default browser.

app/renderer/index.html.role: Desktop app shell markup: empty placeholders the renderer fills from the API's vocabulary, under a Content-Security-Policy that allows nothing but the app's own files.

docs/ROADMAP.md.role: The build plan, the hard constraints and the decision log. Every component, all built and tested.
docs/ROADMAP.md.notes: The decision log is the record of WHY: read it before changing behaviour that looks arbitrary.

docs/runbook.md.role: The operator's page for one tax season: the designated machine and why only one may run a clients root, what a person does each morning and on the draft day, what every index reason and validation note means, and the thirty-minute move to another machine.
docs/runbook.md.notes: Written for a person, not an agent. Roles are docs/workflow.md and the reasons behind the rules are docs/ROADMAP.md; it links to both rather than repeating them.

README.md.role: What the system is, how to run each stage, and how to set it up. Who does what is docs/workflow.md.

requirements.txt.role: Runtime and dev dependencies, pinned exactly (a guard refuses a range); the optional OCR extras are documented here too.
requirements.txt.notes: requirements-build.txt adds the pinned freezer on top for Build App.bat; api_entry.spec is the committed freeze and app/package-lock.json the committed Electron install, so a build is made from the commit rather than from whatever was current that day (decision 46).

requirements-build.txt.role: What Build App.bat installs: requirements.txt plus the pinned PyInstaller.

artifact:_manifest.xlsx.role: The engagement's request list and its live status, plus the Engagement sheet (client, link, due, sender, firm, reminders, active, and the catalog form the list was cut from) the scheduled run reads. Sits OUTSIDE the client's shared scope — the accountant's file, not theirs.

artifact:_index.xlsx.role: Every original the client sent: where it came from, where it went, and what it was renamed to. The audit trail. Its last column, Evidence, says what each candidate request was a candidate on: which of that request's own keywords the document said and where it said them (content_check.format_evidence()), or the code of the reason that refused the file. Catalog words and file names only, never a word of the client's document. Since decision 88 it is written on every pass exactly as before but READ ONLY AS THE FALLBACK: filer.read_index() answers from _ledger.jsonl wherever that record holds an index-shaped event, and reads this workbook where it does not - a folder from before the record, or one whose record holds nothing but a scan. read_index_from_workbook() is this file's own reading, kept public for the record's bootstrap, for _index_records() (asked between a write landing and the record learning of it) and for the suite's agreement fixture. It is still asked one thing whichever way a read answers: whether it is an index the tracker may touch at all (rows and no header row it knows are refused), because it is still rewritten every pass.

artifact:_manifest.pending.json.role: Sidecar holding status updates that could not be written because Excel had the manifest locked. Merged into the next successful write. Written whole or not at all (atomic_replacement); an unreadable one is moved aside only by the write that would retry it, never by a reader or a dry run.

artifact:_index.pending.json.role: A versioned snapshot of the whole _index.xlsx (INDEX_SIDECAR_VERSION) written when Excel had the workbook open: every row, including one a person rewrote. read_index_from_workbook() returns it in the workbook's place until the next successful write lands it. An older bare-list sidecar holds only rows to append after the workbook's and is folded in once. Written whole or not at all; an unreadable one is moved aside only by a real run, never by a reader or a dry run. Decision 88: it is still read whichever way read_index() answers - it may be the only copy of rows the workbook has not taken, an I/O error reading it is never guessed past, and a row it holds that the record has never seen (a bare list, or a snapshot an older version left) is read, said out loud and recorded by the next write.

artifact:_ledger.jsonl.role: The engagement's own append-only record (decision 87): one JSON event per line, in the order the writers wrote them - what was preserved, filed, parked, called a duplicate, decided by a person, had its bytes recorded, taught a keyword, and the statuses each scan applied. Written only under the engagement lock, with O_APPEND and fsync, one line per event and never rewritten; a torn last line is ignored by the reader and truncated by the next append. Since decision 88 it is what the readers BELIEVE: filer.read_index() answers from its fold wherever it holds an index-shaped event and manifest.load_manifest() takes each identifier's scanner columns from it wherever it has recorded one, with the workbooks as the per-row, per-identifier fallback. The workbooks are still written exactly as before, so deleting this file puts the reading back - that is what makes the step reversible. A record that does not read as one falls back to the workbook and says so loudly, naming the engagement and the line. A person never edits it, and `python -m tracker.ledger <folder> --compare` is how a person checks it against the workbooks.

artifact:_content_cache.json.role: Tier-3 verdict cache beside the manifest: pass/fail, reason and the evidence behind it per file, never extracted client text. Disposable - an unreadable one, or one written at an older CACHE_VERSION (the constant in tracker/content_check.py; the evidence column arrived with decision 82), is reset - and written whole or not at all.

artifact:Shared/.role: The client's one drop folder — the only thing they see and the only thing they touch. Their originals end up in Shared/PBC/, still visible to them, untouched.

artifact:Prepared/.role: The firm-side working set: renamed copies sorted per request, plus 00 - Needs Review for anything that could not be identified. The client never sees this.

artifact:reminder-draft.txt.role: The drafted chase email, waiting for a person to read, edit and send. Carries a fingerprint so the weekly job can tell whether it has been edited.

artifact:status.html.role: The practice on one page, in the clients root beside the run log: every engagement with what it owes, the review queue across all of them newest first, and everything that failed. Written by every real pass (STATUS_PAGE_FILENAME in tracker/runner.py) and by the app's own pass; read by a person, who opens it from the clients folder or with the app's Open Status button. One self-contained file - no script, nothing fetched - because it names client files. Never on a dry run.

rule:no-AI-on-client-documents.role: No generative AI ever reads a client financial document. Every routing and status decision comes from deterministic rules in the manifest.

rule:originals-are-never-altered.role: Originals are never altered. Files are moved byte for byte under their own names into Shared/PBC/; all work happens on copies, and every move is recorded in _index.xlsx.

rule:nothing-is-guessed.role: Nothing is guessed. A document is filed only when exactly one request accepts it - or, when one document names several forms as itself, when each of those forms is accepted by exactly one request. Ambiguous, contested and unrecognized files go to 00 - Needs Review for a person - misfiling a tax document is worse than not filing it.

rule:nothing-is-ever-sent.role: Nothing is ever sent. The system drafts client emails and stops. There is no SMTP, no mail client and no network call in the reminder or scheduling path.

Start App.bat.role: Runs the desktop app from source: checks for Python and Node, installs the Electron packages app/package-lock.json pins (`npm ci`, first run only) and starts Electron.
Start App.bat.notes: Electron is started through its own entry script under `node`, never the `npx` shim: the shim breaks when the folder's path contains an ampersand, which the firm's own checkout does (decision 53). Electron downloads its binary on the first start, so the install step needs the network once. Decision 55: installs requirements.txt every start (a second when satisfied).

Build App.bat.role: Builds the portable package: freezes the API with PyInstaller from the committed api_entry.spec inside a virtual environment holding exactly requirements-build.txt, packages the Electron shell with @electron/packager, copies the frozen API into resources/ and writes BUILD-INFO.txt.
Build App.bat.notes: Reproducible from the commit (decision 46): the freeze runs in its own venv because PyInstaller follows optional imports and the machine's Python would otherwise leak unrelated packages into the package (decision 53). The packager runs through its entry script under `node`, not the `npx` shim, for the ampersand reason Start App.bat states; the copy into the package is `robocopy` with its exit code checked and the executable's presence asserted, because `xcopy` gave up on the package's long paths while the script still reported success (decision 53). Guards pin OUT to .gitignore and the resources path to app/main.js. Decision 55: the venv is made fresh each build; no parenthesised value is expanded inside the build-info block. Decision 78: every exit goes through one `:wait` label, which pauses for the person who double-clicked unless TRACKER_BUILD_NONINTERACTIVE is set - the one switch, named in this file's header and read nowhere else, and what lets .github/workflows/build.yml run this file rather than a copy of it.

automation.manifest.json.role: The firm's Command Center integration surface, and the whole of it: the card this tool shows on the office dashboard, and the four actions it offers there - a preview pass, a real pass, the engagement list and the learned keywords. No tracker code reads this file; the Command Center discovers it under its configured roots and runs the argv arrays in it with cwd set to the repository root.
automation.manifest.json.notes: Decision 81. The Center's safety contract refuses any manifest declaring that it schedules itself, and refusing one never stopped a Task Scheduler entry - it only meant this tool stayed off the board or declared a falsehood. The owner's written exception of 2026-09-18 is declared here in safety.scheduled_exception, the dated field the contract gained the same day, and the card prints that sentence; auto_send and money_movement admit no exception, ever. Each action is an argv array, never a shell string, and every flag it names has to exist in the module it calls. The pass takes the clients root as a positional argument rather than reading settings.py, because Task Scheduler and the Center hand the process none of the shell's environment - api_entry.py's rule: the job needs nothing but its command line; tools/learned_keywords.py takes no parameter here and reads the root from the settings file itself. run-pass carries the log flag ahead of a bare -- so the root that follows is read as the positional and not swallowed as the log's optional value.

tracker/page.py.role: The markup both of the firm's pages are drawn with, owned once: esc() (every value on either page goes through it), the table builder (header row in a thead, data in a tbody, headers optionally marked for a page that sorts them), Cell and Row for the few cells and rows that want a class, slug() for a word as a class name, unesc() for reading a value back out of an attribute, and page_text() for the bytes a page is written as.
tracker/page.py.notes: Decision 91. It knows nothing about engagements, manifests or the record - values in, markup out - which is why it imports nothing from the package and both tracker/runner.py (the practice page, decision 75) and tracker/view.py (the engagement's own page) can import it without a cycle. There is deliberately NO helper for a script tag, a style sheet link or an image: a page naming the firm's clients must not reach the network to render, so a page's own style is inline in the module that owns that page. page_text() encodes with backslashreplace for the same reason the run log does - a name NTFS holds is not always one UTF-8 can, and one client's file name must not cost the whole page. api._slug is this module's slug(), so a status chip in the app and a status badge on the view are classed by one function. No dedicated test file: it is covered through the two pages that use it (tests/test_view.py, tests/test_runner.py).

tracker/view.py.role: The page a person opens: VIEW_FILENAME, regenerated in the engagement folder at the end of every real pass from the readers (load_manifest() for the request rows and their statuses, read_index() for the originals, review.triage() for what each parked file might be), in four sections - Summary, Requests, Index, Needs Review. Owns the file name, the Summary's labels and their meta names, the three words a view's state is said in (CURRENT / BEHIND / UNKNOWN), the chip's label and the button's, render_page(), write_view(), view_state(), read_stamp(), the two row builders (request_row(), index_row()) and the CLI that redraws one engagement and prints its state.
tracker/view.py.notes: Decision 89, stage A step 3, as decision 91 settled it: the owner's rule is that every file staff open only to READ is a web page, and the only Excel file they open is the one they edit. IT HOLDS NO FACT, and that is the whole design: no fact is read back - only the stamp in its meta tags, by read_stamp(), for the current / behind / unknown chip - so the one failure every other file must survive costs nothing here. A page whose replace does not land is not replaced, the run carries view_stale and SUCCEEDS, the older page stands and the next pass lands one - no sidecar, no retry, no deferred rows. Written through manifest.write_text_atomically(); there is NO read-only attribute any more (a browser holds no write lock, and an attribute this module set could only trip the next replace), and the _make_writable helper is gone with it. On Windows a plain open() read handle still refuses the replace - Python's open shares reading and writing, never deleting - so view_stale has a real trigger there; on POSIX the replace lands under the reader. Every value goes through page.esc() and the page fetches nothing. The stamp lives in meta tags in the head and read_stamp() reads it with one regular expression - no HTML parser in production - so a label may be reworded for a person without moving a field name under a reader. view_state() compares the stamp's two digests - the rules workbook's SHA-256 (validators.sha256_of, the one digest of bytes in the package) and ledger.head() - with those two things now; it takes no lock and reads the file's bytes, so it answers while somebody has the page open. Section headings come from their owners (manifest.SHEET_NAME, filer.INDEX_SHEET, filer.NEEDS_REVIEW) and the review shortlist's sentences from tracker/review.py, so the page invents no heading and no word of a suggestion. Imports downwards only - ledger, manifest, filer, scaffold, review, page, validators - and only runner and api import it; writing the view is the last thing a pass does. tests/conftest.py draws the page again from the live readers through render_page() after every test and requires the same bytes, with only the clock excluded.

artifact:Status Report.html.role: The page a person opens (decisions 89 and 91), in the engagement folder beside the manifest and the index, and the only file there without a leading underscore because it is the one staff are meant to open. One self-contained HTML file - inline style, no image, no font, nothing fetched - with a sticky navigation and four sections: Summary (the rules workbook's digest, the record's head, when it was drawn in UTC and in local time, the counts, and the sentence that says it holds no facts of its own), Requests (statuses as coloured badges, a waived row dimmed), Index and Needs Review (the parked rows, each with the shortlist review.triage() computes). Every table sorts on a click through a few lines of inline script and is a plain table without it. REGENERATED BY EVERY REAL PASS from the readers, never on a dry run. It HOLDS NO FACT - every value on it is the record's, the manifest's or the index's - so no fact is read back (read_stamp() reads only the stamp) and there is nothing on it to edit. The stamp is in meta tags in the head (tracker-rules-sha256, tracker-record-sha256, tracker-generated and one per Summary field), which view_state() reads with a regular expression. A page whose replace does not land - on Windows an open read handle is enough to refuse it - is simply not replaced: the run reports view_stale and succeeds, and the one on disk stays honestly behind. The app says current / behind / unknown beside the engagement's name (tracker.view.view_state) and opens it with the Open Status Report button; `python -m tracker.view <folder>` redraws one.

artifact:runs.log.role: The one run log in the clients root (LOG_FILENAME in tracker/runner.py): one summary line per pass, appended by a pass run with the log flag - the scheduled task and the Command Center's run-pass action both pass it - never on a dry run, and never read by the system; a person opens it.
